cues.text: A Feast for Every Saint
Each November 1, the Church keeps a feast of all the saints, known and unknown.
The Catholic Encyclopedia says it honors all the saints.
According to Pope Urban IV, it also makes up for any shortcomings in the faithful's keeping of saints' feasts during the year.
Its roots are ancient, for a sermon of St. Ephrem the Syrian already mentions a common day of honor.
In the West, Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon in Rome to the Blessed Virgin and all the martyrs on May 13, 609 or 610.
Later Pope Gregory III consecrated a chapel in St. Peter's Basilica to all the saints and fixed its anniversary for November 1.
Pope Gregory IV extended that celebration to the whole Church.
The evening before is popularly called Halloween.
The Martyrs First
In the earliest days, the Church honored her martyrs.
The faithful guarded their bodies, buried them with honor, and built an altar over each tomb, where they offered Mass in thanksgiving.
That is why an early word for a church was "martyrium," and why the relics of martyrs still rest beneath our altars.
Churches shared accounts of their martyrs with one another, such as the letter from the Church of Smyrna on the martyrdom of St. Polycarp .
To be sure that a martyr was genuine, the Church kept lists of authentic martyrs and forbade public honor to anyone else.
The local bishop judged each case.
Beyond the Martyrs
Honor for saints who were not martyrs seems to have taken root only in the fourth century, and only after long discussion.
Among the earliest confessors honored were the hermits of the desert in the East and St. Martin of Tours in the West.
For centuries, local bishops decided who would be honored in their dioceses.
Often the bishop's approval took the form of moving a saint's body to an honorable place beneath an altar.
The very word "canonize" first meant placing a saint's name in the Canon of the Mass.
Rome Takes the Lead
As abuses arose, the popes took a firmer hand.
The first formal decree of canonization seems to be that of St. Ulrich of Augsburg, which Pope John XV issued at a synod in the Lateran in 993.
That is why this entry stands at that year.
In 1181, Pope Alexander III rebuked a diocese that was honoring a man who had died in a drunken brawl.
No one, he said, could be venerated publicly as a saint without the authority of the Roman Church.
Canonization was gradually reserved to the pope, something formalized under Pope Gregory IX in 1234.
The decrees of Pope Urban VIII, in full force by 1634, forbade public honor to anyone not beatified by the Apostolic See.
In the eighteenth century, Pope Benedict XIV refined the procedures.
How a Saint Is Made
Today a cause begins locally.
Devotion starts with those who knew the person, and the fame of holiness spreads, first regionally and then universally.
The bishop investigates, and the person is called a Servant of God.
When the pope recognizes heroic virtue or martyrdom, the Servant of God is declared Venerable.
For beatification, a miracle is also required, except for martyrs.
A beatification may rest on martyrdom, on heroic virtue, or on the offering of one's life for others.
After beatification the person is called Blessed.
Canonization requires a miracle as well, though popes have occasionally waived it.
With a canonization, the pope solemnly and irrevocably proclaims that the person is in heaven.
A beatification is usually celebrated locally by a papal delegate, while a canonization is typically celebrated in Rome by the pope himself.
Blessed Fulton Sheen shows the steps.
His cause opened in 2002, he was declared Venerable in 2012, and he was beatified on September 24, 2026.
One more approved miracle is needed for canonization.
The Call That Includes Us
Canonization names the few, but the call to holiness reaches everyone.
The Second Vatican Council taught that all the faithful, of whatever rank or status, are called to the fullness of the Christian life.
The Catechism repeats it: all Christians, in any state or walk of life, are called to the perfection of charity.
This April, Pope Leo XIV reminded the faithful that holiness is not a privilege of the few, but a gift that asks every baptized person to strive for the perfection of charity.
The Council added that the forms and tasks of life are many, but holiness is one.
Known and Unknown
That is why the Church keeps this feast.
No earthly list can name every saint.
Beyond those the Church has canonized, there are countless others whose names only God knows.
The saints show us still that holiness is meant for ordinary days in ordinary places, lived by ordinary people with the grace of God.
On this feast we thank the Lord for every one of them, and we ask them to pray for us.
The call that made them saints is the same call that reaches each of us today.
